title: Exploring the associations of physical activity, social anxiety, perceived stress, and quality of life in Chinese college students: A network analysis
content:
by Fumei Yuan, Hong Wang, Wentao Qiu, Chaoliang Mao

College students face complex interactions among physical activity, quality of life, social anxiety, and perceived stress. This study employed network analysis to explore these associations. A cross-sectional sample of 699 Chinese undergraduates (427 males, 272 females) completed the PARS-3, WHOQOL-BREF, PSS-10, and LSAS. A Gaussian graphical model was estimated using EBICglasso; strength, expected influence, and bridge expected influence (BEI) were calculated. Social anxiety and perceived stress were moderately to strongly positively correlated (r = 0.42–0.51), and both were substantially negatively correlated with quality of life, whereas after accounting for conditional dependencies, physical activity occupied a peripheral position, showing only weak partial associations with the psychological variables. “social interaction fear” exhibited the highest strength and EI and emerged as the strongest bridge node (BEI = 1.26). The network density was 58%, and the network exhibited relatively favorable stability. The Network Comparison Test revealed no significant gender differences in global network structure (p = 0.23) or global strength (p = 0.37), suggesting that the fundamental network architecture is consistent across genders. These findings indicate that the associations between physical activity and students’ negative emotions and quality of life are weak at the conditional-dependence level, whereas social anxiety symptoms—particularly “social interaction fear”—constitute the core of this network, providing symptom-level evidence for future longitudinal research.
